models.label: No change
models.description: Carry the current inflation measure forward.

models.label: Autoregression
models.description: Direct OLS forecast using an intercept and the three most recent monthly observations of the inflation measure.

models.label: Autoregression + labour market
models.description: Adds the twelve-month change in the unemployment rate, in percentage points. A rise indicates a weakening labour market. It measures the change in slack, not its equilibrium level.

windows.label: Expanding history
windows.description: Use all eligible monthly training observations up to each forecast origin.

windows.label: Rolling 10 years
windows.description: Use only eligible training outcomes in the last 120 calendar months ending at the origin.

studies.label: Year-on-year inflation · 1 month ahead
studies.definition: Forecast the year-on-year change in the seasonally adjusted CPI index 1 month ahead. The no-change forecast repeats the year-on-year rate at the origin.

studies.label: Year-on-year inflation · 6 months ahead
studies.definition: Forecast the year-on-year change in the seasonally adjusted CPI index 6 months ahead. The no-change forecast repeats the year-on-year rate at the origin.

studies.label: Year-on-year inflation · 12 months ahead
studies.definition: Forecast the year-on-year change in the seasonally adjusted CPI index 12 months ahead. The no-change forecast repeats the year-on-year rate at the origin.

studies.label: New inflation over the next 6 months
studies.definition: Annualized CPI growth over the six months after the origin, 100 × [(CPI(t+6)/CPI(t))² − 1]. The no-change forecast repeats the annualized change from t−6 to t. The two price-change intervals are disjoint.

methods: Each horizon has its own direct regression. Coefficients are re-estimated at every monthly origin. A training pair is eligible only after its target month has been reached. The most recent observed outcome can enter training. Subsequent target values are reserved for scoring.

The origin is a reference month after its CPI and labour-market readings have become available. The experiment uses the pinned ALFRED revision vintage throughout. Historical data releases, their original values and their publication lags are not replayed. These retrospective forecasts cannot be used as a real-time trading record.

Both estimators use identical training rows within a window, including the slack variable. Both windows and all models are scored on exactly matched monthly targets. A rolling window spans 120 calendar months of known target dates and requires at least 100 complete training pairs. Missing levels, lags or test outcomes are never filled.

Evaluation periods refer to the realized target month. A forecast for the first month of a crisis may therefore have been formed beforehand. The financial-crisis window includes December 2007, the NBER peak month, and is an evaluation window rather than a recession label.

MAE is mean absolute error. RMSE is root mean square error. Bias is mean forecast minus outcome. All errors are in percentage points. MAE gain is the no-change benchmark’s MAE minus the model’s MAE on the same targets. A positive gain favours the model.

The 95% intervals use a Bartlett Newey–West estimate for paired absolute-loss differences. Calendar-distance lags preserve gaps. The bandwidth is the larger of horizon minus one and floor[4 × (n/100)^(2/9)], capped at n−1. Small subsamples and persistent model changes limit the precision of these pointwise intervals. Multiple comparisons are unadjusted. The incremental slack comparison subtracts the labour-market model’s absolute error from the autoregression’s absolute error.

Year-on-year inflation shares eleven underlying monthly price changes at horizon one and six at horizon six. At horizon twelve there is no shared price-change interval. The separate six-month fresh-inflation target tests entirely subsequent changes. Neighbouring monthly forecasts of that target overlap each other, so we also score all six possible non-overlapping semiannual grids.

interpretation: In the 1970s, adding the twelve-month change in unemployment to a rolling inflation-only model reduced six-month MAE by 0.21 points. The paired interval was 0.00 to 0.43 points. Both models used the same forecast dates and estimation sample.

From 2022 onward, the rolling labour-market model’s six-month-ahead inflation MAE was 1.49 points, versus 1.07 for no change. Its paired gain interval was -0.82 to -0.02 points. The same labour-market specification with expanding estimation had MAE of 0.94 points.

Across all evaluation months, the rolling labour-market model’s gain over persistence was -0.02 points for six-month-ahead year-on-year inflation and -0.03 for the fresh six-month rate. These are different targets with different persistence benchmarks.

For fresh inflation from 2022 onward, rolling labour-market forecasts beat persistence on 0 of the six disjoint semiannual grids. Each grid had only 7 to 10 outcomes, so this checks sensitivity to the choice of months.

The same six-month rolling model produced an MAE gain of 0.10 during the 2007–09 crisis and -0.23 in the post-crisis evaluation. The crisis comparison contains nineteen target months. Overlap makes it a particularly short test of relative forecasting skill.
